question: The Commission has just brought a case before the EU Court of Justice against wood pigeon hunting in France, which it deems to be contrary to the Birds Directive. In the south-west of France, chiefly in the regions of Occitanie and Nouvelle-Aquitaine, pigeon-hunting hides have been set up for hunting of non-protected species.

They serve as genuine intergenerational meeting spaces in abandoned rural areas that have been left behind by globalisation. The hides also enable maintenance and monitoring the forest and its fauna, and prevent the proliferation of certain birds that can sometimes be harmful to ecosystems.

These include cormorants, whose numbers have spiked by 16% in three years, greatly hindering the reproduction of eels and pike, protected river species. Cormorants are overprotected by partisan animal-protection associations, which put pressure on authorities to stand idly by. 1.
Does the European Commission intend to enshrine traditional hunting, such as wood pigeon hunting in France, as part of Europe's heritage and way of life?
Will it guarantee hunting quotas for invasive bird species despite the influence of partisan associations?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.5.2025) 1. Member States are not prohibited per se from allowing traditional hunting.

However, should a traditional hunting entail the use of a method that is prohibited under Article 8 read in combination with Annex IV of the Birds Directive1, Member States can only allow such hunting if the conditions for a derogation under Article 9 of the Directive are met, in particular the condition that ‘there is no other satisfactory solution’.

In this regard, the Court of Justice of the European Union has consistently ruled that the traditional nature of a hunting method is not in itself sufficient to establish that ‘there is no other satisfactory solution’2. 2. According to the Birds Directive, the Great Cormorant is not a huntable species in the EU.

However, Article 9 of the Directive provides that Member States may issue derogations that allow for the killing of cormorants, amongst others, where they consider that this is necessary to prevent serious damage to crops, livestock, forests, fisheries and water, and provided there is no other satisfactory solution. The power to issue derogation decisions lies solely with the Member States.
In line with the provisions of the Birds Directive, the Commission is not involved in this process and should just be informed ex post.
1 Directive 2009/147/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 November 2009 on the

conservation of wild birds, OJ L 20, 26.1.2010, p. 7–25. 2 For instance Case C-900/19 of 17 March 2021 (point 44): https://curia.europa.eu/juris/document/document.jsf;jsessionid=22B423AD7745CE8CBD40E37F07965C60?text =&docid=238963&pageIndex=0&doclang=EN&mode=lst&dir=&occ=first&part=1&cid=2177923
